solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Poultry farm's hierarchy?

parts.note: read literally, the ranking hens set up among themselves by pecking one another, which gave the everyday phrase for any social ranking

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the literal farmyard meaning is the joke: the phrase began as a description of hens' behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names any ranking of status within a group, and originally described dominance among chickens.

clue.text: Chapter torn from very long book, perfect example

indicators.note: torn from means one piece is ripped out of the longer stretch

parts.note: epic means very long
a tome is a big book

explanation.surface: A chapter ripped out of a huge book, which was otherwise a perfect example of its kind.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is a typical or ideal instance that sums up a whole class.

clue.text: Oh no underwear!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: '...!' is a British exclamation of annoyance

explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'knickers!' is a mild cry of exasperation, much like 'Oh no!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names women's pants and serves as a British interjection of irritation.

clue.text: Requirement in fine editorial

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning them

explanation.surface: A newspaper's requirement for a fine editorial.
explanation.definitionFit: A need is something necessary, so it is a requirement.

clue.text: Where chimney pot may be found for nothing

definitions.text: Where chimney pot may be found
definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally, on top of the building, where chimney pots sit
second meaning: a drink ... is free, paid by the establishment

explanation.walkthrough: The literal phrase locates a chimney pot; the idiom means provided free by a pub or restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means free of charge, given by the business, and literally atop a dwelling.

clue.text: Crackers filled with last of cheddar, rough

indicators.note: filled with means the first word holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: crackers means mad, as does daft

indicators.note: last of means take only the final letter of the next word

parts.note: final letter of cheddar

explanation.surface: Cheese crackers with a cheddar filling that have come out rough.
explanation.definitionFit: A draft is a rough first version, so as an adjective it means preliminary.

clue.text: Admin regulations in dept are ludicrous

indicators.note: ludicrous means absurd, so these letters are thrown into a crazy new order

explanation.surface: A complaint that the paperwork rules in some department are absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is excessive bureaucratic procedure, named after the ribbon once tied round official documents.

clue.text: Mark found under bird tracks — that's a fine thing!

indicators.note: in a down clue, found under means placed below the earlier pieces

parts.note: a cock is a male bird
to tail is to follow or track someone
a tick is a mark on a page

explanation.surface: A mark noticed beneath a bird's footprints, hailed as a fine discovery.
explanation.walkthrough: Fine here means thin, not excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: The item is a slender skewer for olives or cheese, a very thin object.

clue.text: Ordinary old coins

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the high-wheeled bicycle was called an ordinary
second meaning: a penny and a farthing were pre-decimal British coins

explanation.walkthrough: The Victorian high-wheel bicycle was known as an 'ordinary'; a farthing was a quarter of an old penny.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the early bicycle comes from the size contrast of two British coins.

clue.text: Hole, if between gold and diamonds

indicators.note: between means the word if is placed in the middle, flanked by the two other pieces

parts.note: OR is the heraldic word for gold
ice is slang for diamonds
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzle about where a hole might sit in a piece of jewellery set with gold and diamonds.
explanation.definitionFit: An orifice is an opening or aperture, especially one in the body.

clue.text: Rubbish to empty out tomorrow before decay

indicators.note: emptying out a word removes its contents, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: the outer letters of tomorrow
to addle is to go rotten, as an egg does

explanation.surface: A note about putting the rubbish out for tomorrow's collection before it starts to rot.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle is nonsense talk, so it is rubbish in the sense of foolish words.

clue.text: Criticise achievement of batter

definitions.meaning: second meaning: in cricket a ... is a batter's innings

explanation.walkthrough: Batter suggests cooking, but it is the cricketer at the crease; a good innings is called a knock.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for finding fault and a cricket noun for a spell of batting.

clue.text: Moderate break before fall

parts.note: a rest is a break from activity
rain is a fall from the sky

explanation.surface: Advice to take a moderate break before a tumble, as if for a tired walker.
explanation.definitionFit: To moderate something is to hold it in check, as a verb meaning curb.

clue.text: Troubling row with the Lord in the afterlife

indicators.note: troubling suggests stirring up and disturbing, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A troubling quarrel with God after death.
explanation.definitionFit: The otherworld is a realm beyond this one, such as the world of the dead.

clue.text: Departure from the norm a bit rare, on changing

indicators.note: changing means these letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A remark that something being slightly unusual is a departure from what is normal.
explanation.definitionFit: An aberration is a deviation from what is usual or expected.

clue.text: Page — one has a margin

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sheet of a book
second meaning: a plant ... has a margin, the botanical name for its edge

explanation.walkthrough: Both meanings have a margin: a book page and a botanical leaf, whose edge botanists call its margin.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a single sheet of paper in a book and also the green blade of a plant.

clue.text: Composer with part written up for graduate

parts.note: J S Bach, the German composer

indicators.note: in a down clue, written up means read from bottom to top, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: A composer writing a part for a graduate.
explanation.definitionFit: A bachelor is someone holding a first university degree, as in Bachelor of Arts.

clue.text: Grey matter — might one be white or brown?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... is slang for the head or brain, from rhyming slang ... of bread for head

definitions.text: might one be white or brown?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a ... of bread may be white or brown

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'use your loaf' means use your brain, from rhyming slang loaf of bread = head.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses the word for brains, and in everyday terms it is a baked unit of bread.

clue.text: Stuffy serials broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: A view that serials on TV or radio are stuffy.
explanation.definitionFit: An airless room lacks fresh air, so it is close and stuffy.

clue.text: Person taking photos of a communist swimmer

parts.note: a red is a communist
a snapper is a photographer

explanation.surface: A photographer whose subject is a communist.
explanation.definitionFit: The red snapper is a fish, and a fish is a swimmer in crossword terms.

clue.text: Image picking up previous credit

indicators.note: picking up means the first word gathers the other inside it

parts.note: pic is short for picture
last means previous, as in last week

explanation.surface: A picture collecting earlier credit, as if for a photographer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastic is informal for credit cards, and so for paying on credit.

clue.text: Go towards the cellar perhaps for refuse

definitions.meaning: first meaning: read literally, to ... is to head downwards, as towards a cellar
second meaning: to ... an offer is to decline it

explanation.walkthrough: Refuse looks like a noun meaning rubbish; it is the verb, decline.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to decline or reject, and literally to take a downward turn.

clue.text: Satan existed, looking from the abyss?

indicators.note: in a down clue, looking up from the abyss means reading upward, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: lived means existed

explanation.surface: Satan was real, peering up out of the bottomless pit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Devil is the chief evil spirit of Christian belief, another name for Satan.

clue.text: PM fell, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Edward ..., British Prime Minister 1970 to 1974
second meaning: a fell is upland moor

explanation.walkthrough: Fell looks like a verb (the PM fell from power); it is a northern English word for a moorland hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Heath was a Conservative Prime Minister, and a heath is open moorland like a fell.

clue.text: Long time in embrace of scallywag especially

indicators.note: in embrace of means the letters are held inside the following words, spanning them

explanation.surface: A long hug from a rascal in particular.
explanation.definitionFit: Ages is informal for a very lengthy period, as in waiting for ages.

clue.text: Chopper heading for Cardiff, one departing

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, so take the start of the next word

parts.note: first letter of Cardiff
a leaver is someone who leaves

explanation.surface: A helicopter flying to Cardiff while someone leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleaver is a heavy knife for chopping meat, so it is a chopper; the surface suggests a helicopter.

clue.text: Setter for example reflected on classical language

indicators.note: reflected means read as in a mirror, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example
Latin is the language of ancient Rome

explanation.surface: A crossword setter musing on Latin, as setters sometimes do.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelatin makes jellies firm, so it is a setting agent; the surface suggests the puzzle's compiler.

clue.text: OK laid across ground, very secure

indicators.note: ground means crushed and broken up, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Something laid flat across the ground is held very firmly in place.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something entirely stable and dependable, like stone.
